issues.issue: This recital defines "System(s)" as including the "In Balance Muscle Testing Protocols," whereas the operative definition in Section 1 says "ARP Muscle Testing Protocols." The recital and the operative definition describe the licensed property differently.

The recital subjects the license to Licensor's "ongoing monitoring, revision, upgrading, customizing, updating and modification" in its "sole and absolute discretion," which has no counterpart obligation or limit in the operative text. Whether that discretion is an operative term is open.

The recital describes the license as of the System(s) "set forth in Section 2 below," but Section 2 grants only three named items, narrower than the System(s) definition in Section 1. Recital and operative grant point at different scopes.

The definition ends with the open catch-alls "all other intellectual property associated with" the named protocols, "related programs, and related intellectual property," giving the enumerated specifics no controlling effect. What falls inside "System(s)" — the pivot for the confidentiality and post-termination duties — cannot be bounded.

The defined term names the "ARP Muscle Testing Protocols" while the recital that introduces the same defined term names the "In Balance Muscle Testing Protocols," and Section 2 grants a still narrower list. The instrument uses one label for three different bodies of material.

"ARP Therapy Protocol Limited" is an undefined item and the word "Limited" gives no discernible restriction; "60 Minutes a month specialist support" is likewise unelaborated. What was actually licensed cannot be read off the grant.

The three listed items do not match the page 1 package, which promises Loosening and Recovery Protocols plus "Protocols as needed for personal injury, or rehab" and one hour per month of Licensor's time. The grant and the front page describe different bargains.

Rights are said to be "forfeitable in the event of certain circumstances or occurrences as herein set forth" without identifying which circumstances, leaving the forfeiture trigger to be assembled from elsewhere. "Certain circumstances" has no ascertainable content.

"In the event of such assignment, provided Licensee is afforded notice ..., this Licensor shall then have no responsibility or liability" is garbled and it is unclear whether the released party is the assignor or the assignee. The release's scope turns on that reading.

The clause says telephone consultation and email support "shall be provided in accordance with Section 5 below," but Section 5 is Term and Termination and says nothing about support. The cross-reference is broken, leaving the support obligation without content.

The only stated support here is monthly Minneapolis seminars, which does not match the page 1 promise of one hour per month of Licensor's time or the Section 2 grant of "60 Minutes a month specialist support." The extent of Licensor's support duty is inconsistent across the instrument.

The duty to keep "all System(s)" strictly confidential and not to "disclose, display ... or otherwise make available" them to any other party is hard to reconcile with the Section 2 license to use protocols on clients, which necessarily involves displaying them. The two provisions pull in opposite directions on ordinary licensed use.

"Strictly confidential" is applied to the System(s) with no carve-out for information already public or independently known, so the boundary of the obligation is unmarked. What counts as a prohibited display is left at large.

The provision refers to "Block A of Page 1," which is not a labelled block on page 1, and it grants renewal rights to the "Lessee" of "this lease" inside a license agreement. The term and the renewal right cannot be applied as written.

The license term is keyed to the page 1 start date, whereas Lease paragraph 1 starts the term on the first day of the month following shipment for the same Block A period. The two agreements executed together run on different clocks.

"The covenants and provisions herein set forth shall survive such termination, except those covenants as pertaining to future payments" makes essentially the whole agreement perpetual with no stated end. Whether obligations such as the use restrictions truly survive indefinitely is a live question.

If everything survives under this clause, Section 10.3's separate statement that confidentiality and non-disclosure provisions survive is surplusage, and Section 10.1's automatic revocation and reassignment of "any rights herein set forth" points the other way. The survival regime cannot be harmonised.

Limb (ii) triggers automatic termination on "any Licensee attempt to disclose, display, pledge, sell and transfer the System(s)," where the conjunctive "and" would require all of those acts together though "or" is plainly intended. The trigger's reach turns on that conjunction.

Default arises "if Licensor deems itself insecure," a wholly subjective trigger with no standard, and the remedies close with the catch-all "any other remedy at law or in equity" after five specific ones. Both leave the operative boundary to be construed.

"Venue for the enforcement of this Agreement" does not say whether it reaches only contract claims or also related trade secret and tort claims arising from the licensed System(s). The clause's subject-matter scope is the standard battleground.

This clause makes the License Agreement the entire agreement "regarding the subject matter hereof," while Lease paragraph 18 says the Lease is the entire agreement between the parties and paragraph 12 treats the two as cross-defaulting. Whether the documents form one bargain or two exclusive ones is unresolved.

Notices here must go by facsimile or overnight courier, whereas Lease paragraph 22 authorises personal delivery, telegram or first class mail for the companion instrument, and the Section 8 licensee block gives a name with no address or fax number. Valid notice differs between two documents signed at once.

The disclaimer excludes "warranties of marketability," evidently a mistake for merchantability, and then sweeps in "any warranties at common law" without limit. Which implied warranties are actually disclaimed depends on reading through the error.

The clause waives all claims "except for any breach or breaches of Licensor's contractual obligations," then in the next sentence waives all rights to claim fraud or to seek "any form of redress with respect to said property." The carve-out and the second waiver overlap and cannot both be given full effect.

"Any rights herein set forth shall be deemed to be automatically revoked and automatically reassigned to Licensor" does not say whose rights, and rights never assigned to Licensee cannot be "reassigned." The operative effect of the sentence is uncertain.

Automatic revocation of "any rights herein set forth" on termination is difficult to square with Section 5.2, under which the covenants and provisions of the agreement survive termination. The instrument both extinguishes and preserves the same rights.

The obligation to return "all copies or renditions or enhancements" of the System(s) presupposes tangible deliverables, while Section 1 defines System(s) as protocols, trade secrets and intellectual property generally. What must physically be returned is not identifiable from the definition.

Singling out confidentiality and non-disclosure provisions for post-termination survival invites an expressio unius reading against Section 5.2, which already makes all covenants survive except future payment obligations. The two survival clauses cannot both be given their natural effect.

The clause binds the user to "the instructions contained in the ARP Unit Manual" and its "Cautionary and Warning language," a document neither defined nor attached. The content of the obligation lies wholly outside the agreement.
